rv.q: Mostly, Eldridge and co make the case for the 62-year-old novel’s enduring appeal, with Keenan’s study in disillusionment crossed with dogged determination really clinching the deal.
This stage adaptation is a worthy addition to the canon.
Fans of spy shenanigans and Cold War political machinations will be instantly swept up in this lean, pacy adaptation.
Le Carre’s plot still snakes craftily to its wintry conclusion: that intelligence services are driven by a single moral imperative - results.
Yet neither survive intact in Eldridge’s new play, however niftily he condenses the book’s labyrinthian twists and turns.
There is much to enjoy, particularly for Le Carré aficionados, and it's a noble effort to show that his densely detailed novels are stageable.

Carré’s enthralling plot is deftly adapted for the stage by Eldridge, brought to life under Herrin’s meticulous direction, creating a captivating examination of betrayal, love and the high stakes nature of Alec’s last assignment.
It is to Le Carré’s credit that this fundamentally nihilistic thesis makes for cracking reading – and, in the end, a suitably thrilling stage play.
This has still been a tale exhilaratingly told, and if it fails it fails for being too inventive in developing Smiley’s character, rather than not inventive enough.
It’s a good show, but at a little over two hours there is space for a deeper investment in the Leamas–Liz relationship.
Many of them are well-acted, but the tone feels inconsistent and the invitation to invest emotionally half-hearted.
Herrin's production digs deep into an era now passing into distant memory, without making it feel unreachable.
Long-time lovers of his work will find a lot to love about this, but I wonder how much those less familiar would feel?

cn.t: Le Carré's first stage adaptation receives mixed reviews, with critics praising its gripping style and strong performances but criticizing its brisk pace that sacrifices atmosphere and ambiguity for plot clarity.
